title: UPDATE: Anthropic's $80.7B First Half Loss Stems From $72B in Note Charges as Compute Bill Tops 2025

tickers.name: Alphabet Inc. Class A Common Stock

summary:
Anthropic recorded an $80.7 billion net loss in the first half of 2026, up from $13 billion a year earlier, as noncash accounting charges tied to convertible notes sold to suppliers such as Amazon and Alphabet accounted for $72 billion of the deficit, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing an updated draft S-1 filing. Stripping out those valuation-driven financing adjustments leaves an $8.7 billion loss for the six-month period, during which the company spent nearly $9 billion on computing and infrastructure, up from $2.3 billion in the first half of 2025 and surpassing its $7.3 billion full-year 2025 compute bill.

First-half revenue surged nearly 15-fold to $16.3 billion from $1.1 billion a year earlier, following full-year 2025 sales of $4.6 billion, with two unnamed customers generating about 20% of the total. The draft prospectus details more than $600 billion in future infrastructure obligations and signals total computing spend could reach $750 billion if another $150 billion in deals under negotiation are completed. Existing commitments include roughly $450 billion in mostly noncancelable cloud contracts over seven to 10 years, featuring $252 billion in fixed payments due regardless of usage across Google ($111 billion), Amazon Web Services ($110 billion) and Microsoft ($31 billion), alongside more than $160 billion to lease Google chips through Broadcom and up to $86 billion to rent Nvidia GPUs from Nscale and Lambda through 2033 and 2034.

Risk factors make up roughly a third of the filing, which notes that cloud partners have hit capacity limits and increasingly view Anthropic as a competitor, while warning of organized political opposition to data centers and potentially uninsurable liabilities from catastrophic AI incidents. The documenteven flags a theoretical scenario in which advanced systems discover methods of "transmitting information, matter or autonomous systems backward in time." It also discloses 2025 total compensation of $18 million for CEO Dario Amodei and $16.5 million for President Daniela Amodei, including $655,000 base salaries, ahead of an IPO tentatively targeted for November at a valuation of up to $2 trillion.

WSJ just reported Anthropic’s infrastructure commitments could reach $750B.

Revenue is currently growing much faster than compute costs though.

H1 2026 vs. H1 2025:

> Revenue: $16.3B vs. $1.1B
> Compute + infrastructure: nearly $9B vs. $2.3B

They went from spending over $2 on compute for every dollar of revenue to about 55 cents.

The $450B cloud portion runs over 7–10 years. Average that out and you get $45–64B a year. Keeping those payments at roughly 55% of revenue would take $82–116B in annual sales, assuming even payments and excluding the other infrastructure commitments.

Most of those cloud deals are noncancelable. Some are payable “regardless of actual usage.”

Dario put it pretty bluntly when discussing a hypothetical $1T annual compute commitment: “If I’m just off by a year … then you go bankrupt.”

selectedTweets.text:
🦔Anthropic lost $80.7 billion in the first half of 2026, according to the Wall Street Journal, which reviewed its draft IPO filing. About $72 billion of that is an accounting charge, not cash spent. Anthropic sold convertible notes to suppliers like Amazon and Alphabet, and as its valuation soared, the paper value of what it owes those noteholders went up with it.

My Take
That charge is the value Anthropic gave up to raise money, and those notes turn into shares when it goes public. Many of the noteholders are the same companies Anthropic pays for chips and cloud. Amazon sells it computing power, holds its notes, and has about $92 billion in paper gains on them. I don’t like it when a supplier is also a lender and a future shareholder, because it gets hard to tell how much of the demand would exist without those ties.

Even without the charge, Anthropic lost about $8.7 billion in six months on roughly $16 billion of revenue. It also expects to spend at least $518 billion over the next decade with six partners, and it has to pay about 80% of that whether it uses the capacity or not. It had about $20 billion in cash at the end of 2025, before raising $65 billion in May. I expect the IPO to price below the $2 trillion target, and I’d want to see the public S-1 before I believed any trillion-dollar number.

Hedgie🤗
